conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling during the past seven days so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve in these early weeks of motherhood. Everything you share stays confidential between you, me, and the clinical team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you today. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions conversationally; if any feel difficult, we can pause or slow the pace. Shall we start?

Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… not very much. I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would joke around every night—but lately even the things he says that I know are funny just feel… flat. I might smile, but a real laugh? Maybe once or twice the whole week, and even then it felt forced.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I can’t really laugh at all. I might manage a little chuckle here or there, but it feels like work—like I’m making myself do it, not actually feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it’s like, “what’s the point?” I still do them because I know I should, but that spark of looking forward to anything is pretty much gone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I didn’t hold him the right way, or I’m just not a good mom. Even when my husband says it’s normal, I still feel like I should be able to fix it, and I end up replaying everything in my head and feeling guilty.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes—pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing right, or I’ll lie awake picturing horrible things that could happen if I fall asleep. There’s no real reason, but the worry just barges in and I can’t shake it for a while, even when I tell myself it’s irrational.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a tightness in my chest out of nowhere—like I’m about to open the door to something awful, even if I’m just sitting on the couch with the baby monitor next to me. It passes after a few minutes, but those waves of panic show up most days, and I can’t point to any real danger.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time. Dishes pile up, the baby needs something the second I think I have a free moment, and I feel like I’m drowning in little tasks. I still get through the essentials, but it’s exhausting—like I’m always one step behind and about to drop everything.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll finally get the baby down, crawl into bed myself, but my mind just keeps spinning—replaying every little thing I think I messed up, worrying something bad will happen if I fall asleep. Some nights I’m awake for hours before I drift off, and even then I wake up at every tiny sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like a gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be doing something routine—folding laundry, warming a bottle—and this wave of sadness just hits. Sometimes I cry, sometimes I just feel empty, but the happy feelings seem really far away.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened maybe three or four times this week. Sometimes it’s triggered—like when the baby won’t settle and I feel useless—but other times the tears just come out of nowhere, sitting on the couch feeling overwhelmed and suddenly I’m sobbing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind. I just want to feel like myself again and be a good mom.

It sounds as though the joy and spark you once felt has been replaced by a heavy, gray cloud that follows you through each day. You described laughter feeling forced, excitement about simple pleasures gone, and a constant drumbeat of worry and self-blame that leaves you exhausted yet unable to rest. Despite these overwhelming feelings you remain devoted to your baby, motivated only by the wish to feel like yourself again and to be the mother you want to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh naturally most days, aligning with 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('happens a lot') and gives multiple examples of excessive guilt over normal infant behavior, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily intrusive anxiety with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, sudden waves of panic with physical symptoms, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most of the time," unable to keep up with daily tasks, and nearing collapse—closely matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple nights this week of prolonged sleep-onset delay due to racing, distressing thoughts, plus frequent night waking—clearly "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily pervasive sadness and emotional emptiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying 3-4 times this week, both triggered and spontaneous, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 25 far exceeds the 14-point cut-off that flags probable major depression; high scores on Q1,2,3,4,6,7,8 indicate loss of pleasure, self-blame, anxiety, feeling unable to cope, sadness, and insomnia, all aligning with DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset. Combined endorsement of near-daily <sym>panic attacks</sym> and intrusive worries supports comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. Patient denies self-harm, meeting safety screen criteria, but functional impairment is pronounced. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Bring this EPDS result to facilitate discussion; ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>, and whether <med>sertraline</med> or another <med>SSRI</med> is appropriate for you
3. Arrange practical support-partner, family, or postpartum doula-to help with night feeds so you can obtain 4-6 hour blocks of uninterrupted sleep
4. Try brief, scheduled worry times and grounding techniques (e.g., 5-4-3-2-1) when <sym>panic</sym> arises; practice slow diaphragmatic breathing for 2 min during distress
5. Limit self-blame: keep a simple daily log of small parenting wins to counter the <sym>negative thoughts</sym> such as <quote>I'm not a good mom</quote>
6. Join a local or online <med>postpartum support group</med> for peer validation and coping strategies
7. Arrange follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after interventions begin
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary  

<sym>Low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, intrusive anxiety, panic episodes, emotional lability, sleep disruption, feeling overwhelmed.</sym>  

<med>Significant indications for postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety.</med>  

**Risk factors identified**  
- Persistent sadness and tearfulness (daily, multiple crying spells this week)  
- Marked loss of pleasure/interest in usual activities  
- Self-blame and guilt (“not a good mom”) disproportionate to events  
- Unwarranted anxiety and panic (daily racing heart, chest tightness, catastrophic worries)  
- Sleep impairment linked to ruminating and hypervigilance  
- Feeling unable to cope with routine tasks  

**Safety screen:** Denies self-harm ideation; no suicidal thoughts reported.  

**Clinical impression:** Responses meet screening threshold for moderate–severe postpartum depression with co-occurring anxiety; high distress and impaired daily functioning noted. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment and follow-up care planning.
